summary: Describes a schema for storing user passwords in an LDAP directory, including the authPassword attribute type. It supports password-based user authentication with stored values that can use different schemes. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is a rule for how to write down locked-up secret passwords in a big phone book so they can be checked later.

questions: how to store passwords in ldap
subtitle: A schema for storing cryptographically hashed passwords in LDAP directories

tldr.problem: LDAP directories traditionally use the userPassword attribute which must store passwords in cleartext, creating a security risk if the directory is compromised.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3112 defines the authPassword attribute type that stores passwords as cryptographic one-way hashes (using MD5 or SHA1) along with a salt, and provides matching rules so LDAP servers can still authenticate users without exposing the hashes.
tldr.outcome: LDAP administrators can now protect stored passwords from exposure even if the directory is breached, making LDAP authentication systems more secure than cleartext password storage.

today: RFC 3112 is an Informational standard that defines how LDAP servers can store and verify hashed passwords securely. While newer algorithms like bcrypt and scrypt provide better resistance to modern attacks, the authPassword schema remains the standard for password storage in LDAP directories and is supported by major LDAP server implementations.

sections.title: Authentication Passwords in LDAP
sections.content:
The LDAP Authentication Password Schema provides a way to store authentication credentials securely in a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) directory. Instead of storing cleartext passwords like the older userPassword attribute requires, authPassword stores cryptographic hashes derived from passwords, plus additional metadata needed to verify login attempts.

The RFC defines the schema components needed for this: a special syntax for storing hashed values, matching rules that let the server compare an asserted password against stored hashes, and support for multiple hashing schemes so administrators can choose the protection level that fits their needs.
sections.eli5: LDAP is like a phone book database. Instead of writing down actual passwords like "mary123", it scrambles them with special math (a hash function) and stores the scrambled version. That way if someone steals the phone book, they cannot use the passwords.

sections.title: Schema Definitions and Components
sections.content:
The RFC defines several LDAP schema components. The authPasswordSyntax defines the format for storing hashed passwords: it holds three pieces of data: a scheme name (like "MD5" or "SHA1"), an authInfo field (usually the salt in base64 encoding), and an authValue field (the actual hash in base64 encoding). Together they look like MD5$c2FsdA==$...hash....

Two matching rules support password validation: authPasswordExactMatch allows exact comparison of stored values, and authPasswordMatch lets clients assert that a cleartext password matches a stored hash by testing it through the appropriate scheme. The authPassword attribute holds the actual hashed password values on a user entry, and the authPasswordObject class marks entries that may contain password data.
sections.eli5: The schema is the rulebook for how to write down scrambled passwords. It says what fields go in the record (the scramble method name, the salt, the scrambled password), how to format them, and how to check if a guess matches what is stored.

sections.title: Hashing Schemes
sections.content:
The RFC defines two password hashing schemes. In the MD5 scheme, the server concatenates the user's cleartext password with a salt (a random value), computes the MD5 digest of that concatenation, and stores the base64-encoded digest. The salt must be at least 64 bits long and stored in the authInfo field. To check a login attempt, the server reads the stored salt, concatenates it with the asserted password, computes MD5 again, and compares the digests.

The SHA1 scheme works the same way but uses SHA-1 hashing instead of MD5. Both schemes include the salt in the stored value so the server has it available for verification. The RFC recommends servers support SHA1 (required) and optionally support MD5. Servers can use these schemes in conjunction with other authentication methods like Kerberos.
sections.eli5: MD5 and SHA1 are scrambling recipes. They mix the password with a random scramble-key (salt), run special math on it, and get scrambled output. When someone logs in, the server scrambles their guess the same way and checks if the results match.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
LDAP servers implementing this RFC face several decisions. A server may restrict which schemes apply to a particular authentication, but should check all scheme values of selected types when validating a password: if the asserted password matches any stored value of a selected scheme, authentication succeeds. Servers can also use authPassword alongside other storage methods like userPassword or external password stores, giving administrators flexibility in transition.

Both clients and servers SHOULD NOT transmit authPassword values or authPasswordMatch assertions unless the connection uses confidentiality protection like TLS, since even a hashed password should be guarded like a cleartext secret. Servers MUST also protect against abuse: the authPasswordMatch matching rule could be used to mount password-guessing attacks, so access controls and rate limiting are essential. Some schemes require CPU-intensive operations (especially salted hashing), so servers should protect against denial-of-service attacks that exploit this.
sections.eli5: When turning on this feature, administrators need to make sure connections use encryption (like TLS), set up limits so someone cannot guess passwords by trying millions of them, and allow the system time to do the scrambling math without freezing.

sections.title: Security Properties and Risks
sections.content:
The authPassword attribute offers protection against disclosure attacks but requires careful handling. If hashes are exposed, attackers cannot recover the original password immediately like they could with cleartext, but they might attack the hashes using dictionary attacks, rainbow tables, or brute force if the salt is weak. The RFC states that hashed values SHOULD be protected as if they were cleartext passwords, because flaws in the hash function or the salt's randomness could allow recovery.

One-way hashing is an additional security layer, not a complete solution. A user could have multiple passwords stored in the same attribute, creating a risk: if an attacker gains write access, they could store a new password without disabling the original. The RFC recommends using policy-aware clients and servers to prevent this. Servers should also use a scheme-selection configuration that lets them quickly disable a scheme if a vulnerability is discovered, allowing deployment of fixes without changing all stored values.
sections.eli5: Even scrambled passwords need protection because someone might use a big guess-list (like all words in a dictionary) to find the password. If the salt is too short or predictable, attackers can pre-compute answers for many guesses. And if someone hacks in and can write new data, they could add a password of their own to a user account.
